questions.stem: What are the three functions of the urinary system?
questions.why: The urinary system controls discharge of waste filtered from the blood by the kidneys. Its three functions are controlling fluid balance, filtering and eliminating wastes, and controlling pH balance.

options.t: Fluid balance, waste removal, pH control

options.why: Temperature control is not a urinary function.
Absorption of nutrients is a digestive function.
Glucose storage is a liver function.

questions.stem: What are the four components of the urinary system?
questions.why: The components are the kidneys, the ureters, the urinary bladder, and the urethra.

options.why: Those are regions of the kidney, not system components.
The adrenals are endocrine glands sitting on the kidneys.
Nephrons are structures within the kidney, not a component.

questions.stem: How do the kidneys help maintain homeostasis?
questions.why: The kidneys regulate composition, pH, and volume of extracellular fluid. They do it by removing metabolic wastes from the blood and diluting them with water and electrolytes, forming the urine they then excrete.

options.t: By filtering lymph before it rejoins the blood
options.why: Lymph is filtered by lymph nodes.

options.t: By producing the hormones that move all fluid
options.why: They secrete some hormones but do not control all fluid.

options.t: By storing electrolytes until they are needed
options.why: The kidneys excrete excess electrolytes rather than store them.

questions.stem: Which two hormones are secreted by the kidneys?
questions.why: Erythropoietin (EPO) and calcitriol are the hormones secreted by the kidneys. Erythropoietin is the one that drives red blood cell production in the bone marrow.

options.why: Those act on the kidney but are made elsewhere.
Those come from the pancreas.
Renin is renal but cortisol is adrenal.

questions.stem: How do the kidneys primarily regulate arterial blood pressure?
questions.why: The kidneys primarily regulate blood pressure by excreting large amounts of sodium and water — controlling volume controls pressure.

options.t: By secreting erythropoietin to change blood volume
options.why: Erythropoietin governs red cell production.

options.t: By excreting large amounts of sodium and water
By constricting and dilating the renal arteries
options.why: Vessel calibre affects filtration more than systemic pressure.

options.t: By adjusting the glomerular filtration rate alone
options.why: Filtration rate is a means, not the primary mechanism named.

questions.stem: Under what circumstance do the kidneys produce new glucose, and from what?
questions.why: During prolonged fasting the kidneys produce new glucose from amino acids and other chemicals.

options.why: Lactate recycling occurs mainly in the liver.

options.t: During prolonged fasting, from amino acids

options.why: Filtered glucose is reabsorbed, not newly made.

options.t: After every meal, from stored glycogen
options.why: Glycogen breakdown is a liver function after meals.

questions.stem: What are the three distinct internal areas of the kidney?
questions.why: The kidney divides internally into the renal cortex (lighter-colored outer layer closest to the fibrous capsule), the renal medulla (middle layer forming the renal pyramids), and the renal pelvis.

options.t: Renal cortex, renal medulla, and renal pelvis

options.why: Those are parts of the nephron.

options.t: Renal capsule, renal cortex, and renal pyramid
options.why: The capsule and pyramids are not among the three named areas.

options.t: Renal artery, renal vein, and ureter
options.why: Those are vessels and ducts, not kidney regions.

questions.stem: What does the renal pelvis do?
questions.why: The renal pelvis collects urine and forms the upper portion of the ureter. The fibrous capsule is the structure that envelops the kidney and protects it against infection.

options.t: Filters blood arriving from the renal artery
options.why: Filtration happens in the glomerulus.

options.t: Houses the nephrons that reabsorb water
options.why: Nephrons sit in the cortex.
That is the fibrous capsule's role.

options.t: Collects urine and forms the upper ureter

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of the body's systemic cardiac output flows through the kidney each minute?
questions.why: About one-fourth of the body's systemic cardiac output flows through the kidney each minute — which is why renal perfusion is so sensitive to shock. Blood arrives from the abdominal aorta by way of the renal artery.

options.why: That overstates renal blood flow.
That would leave too little for the rest of the body.
That understates renal blood flow.

questions.stem: The renal medulla forms cone-shaped areas. What are they called, and what separates them?
questions.why: The renal medulla is the middle layer and forms cone-shaped areas called renal pyramids, which are separated by renal columns.

options.t: Renal pyramids, separated by renal columns
Renal lobules, separated by fibrous capsules
options.why: Lobules are not the named subdivision.

options.t: Renal calyces, separated by the renal pelvis
options.why: Calyces collect urine rather than forming the cones.

options.t: Renal columns, separated by renal pyramids
options.why: The two terms are reversed here.

questions.stem: What is the functional unit of the kidney, and roughly how many are in each kidney?
questions.why: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, and there are about 1 million nephrons in a kidney. They are found in the cortex.

options.t: The nephron — about 1 million per kidney
The renal pyramid — about 12 per kidney
options.why: Pyramids are gross structures, not functional units.

options.t: The collecting duct — about 10,000 per kidney
options.why: Collecting ducts receive from many nephrons.
The glomerulus is one part of a nephron.

questions.stem: What are the components of a nephron, in order?
questions.why: A nephron contains the glomerulus, the glomerular (Bowman) capsule surrounding it, the proximal convoluted tubule, the loop of Henle, and the distal convoluted tubule, which connects with the collecting tubules.

options.t: Glomerulus, loop of Henle, proximal convoluted tubule, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct
options.why: The loop of Henle comes after the proximal tubule.

options.t: Glomerulus, glomerular capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule
Renal pelvis, glomerulus, tubule, loop of Henle, ureter
options.why: The renal pelvis and ureter come after the nephron.

options.t: Glomerular capsule, glomerulus, distal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, proximal convoluted tubule
options.why: The glomerulus sits inside the capsule, and the order is reversed.

questions.stem: What three things do nephrons do?
questions.why: Nephrons filter the blood, collect excreted water and waste products, and reabsorb water, nutrients, and electrolytes.

options.t: Reabsorb, secrete acid, and make EPO
options.why: Erythropoietin production is a separate kidney function.
Temperature regulation is not a nephron role.

options.t: Filter, make hormones, and store urine
options.why: Urine is stored in the bladder, not the nephron.

questions.stem: Blood enters and leaves the glomerulus by which vessels?
questions.why: Blood enters the glomerulus by an afferent arteriole and leaves by an efferent arteriole — afferent arrives, efferent exits.

options.t: It enters by an efferent arteriole and leaves by an afferent arteriole
options.why: Afferent arrives and efferent exits, not the reverse.

options.t: It enters by the renal artery and leaves by the renal vein directly
options.why: The renal artery branches long before the glomerulus.

options.t: It enters by a capillary and leaves by a venule
options.why: Glomerular vessels are arterioles on both sides.

options.t: It enters by an afferent arteriole and leaves by an efferent arteriole

questions.stem: What allows blood to be filtered in the glomerulus?
questions.why: Pores in the walls of the capillaries in the glomerulus allow the blood to be filtered. Filtered water and wastes — the filtrate — then flow from the glomerular capsule through the renal tubules.

options.t: Osmotic pull generated by the loop of Henle
options.why: The loop concentrates urine after filtration.

options.t: Pores in the glomerular capillary walls
Peristaltic squeezing of the renal pelvis
options.why: Peristalsis moves urine but does not filter.

options.t: Active transport pumps in the tubule wall
options.why: Active transport occurs later, in the tubules.

questions.stem: What does the filtration membrane of the glomerular capsule prevent?
questions.why: The glomerular capsule is a double-layered cup whose inner layer surrounds the glomerular capillaries. Its filtration membrane prevents large molecules such as proteins from entering — which is why protein in the urine signals glomerular damage.

options.why: Filtering waste is the whole point of the membrane.
Electrolytes are filtered and then selectively reabsorbed.
Water passes freely into the capsule.

questions.stem: What is the glomerular filtration rate, and what converts filtrate into urine?
questions.why: Glomerular filtration rate is the amount of filtrate produced. As that filtrate passes through the rest of the nephron, tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion convert it into urine.

options.why: Blood volume entering is not the same as filtrate produced.

options.t: Urine flow rate; peristalsis in the ureter
options.why: Urine flow through the ureter is a later step.
Reabsorption converts filtrate but is not the rate itself.

questions.stem: Which two hormones primarily control the final adjustments to urine composition at the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct?
questions.why: ADH and aldosterone control the final adjustments. ADH increases permeability to water; aldosterone increases active reabsorption of sodium and chloride ions into the blood, with a corresponding increase in water reabsorption.

options.why: Those are secreted by the kidney rather than acting on it.
Renin starts the cascade but does not act at the tubule.
Those regulate blood glucose.

questions.stem: What specifically does ADH do at the distal convoluted tubule and collecting ducts?
questions.why: ADH increases the permeability of those structures to water — more permeable means more water reabsorbed and less urine produced.

options.why: Potassium secretion is aldosterone-driven.
That is aldosterone's action.
ADH acts on the tubule, not on filtration rate.

questions.stem: Where does additional reabsorption of water and electrolytes occur before the filtrate reaches the distal convoluted tubule?
questions.why: Additional reabsorption of water and electrolytes occurs in the loop of Henle. After leaving it, the fluid enters the distal convoluted tubule.

options.why: That comes after the distal tubule.
That is where filtrate is first collected.
That collects finished urine.

questions.stem: Urea is the result of which process, and what does its plasma concentration reflect?
questions.why: Urea results from amino acid catabolism, and its plasma concentration reflects the amount of protein in the diet.

options.why: Carbohydrates are not the source of urea.
Fat metabolism yields ketones, not urea.
That produces uric acid.

questions.stem: What proportion of urea is reabsorbed rather than excreted?
questions.why: About 80% of urea is reabsorbed and the remainder is excreted in the urine.

options.why: That overstates reabsorption.
That is the fraction excreted rather than reabsorbed.
That understates reabsorption.

questions.stem: Uric acid is a result of the metabolism of what?
questions.why: Uric acid results from metabolism of certain organic bases in nucleic acids. Urea is the one that comes from amino acid catabolism.

options.why: Fat breakdown does not yield uric acid.
That produces urea.
Glycogen breakdown yields glucose.

questions.stem: Urine is approximately what percentage water, and what does it usually contain?
questions.why: Urine is about 95% water and usually contains urea and uric acid.

options.t: About 95% water, usually containing urea and uric acid
About 70% water, usually containing urea and bilirubin
options.why: That understates the water fraction.

options.t: About 80% water, usually containing protein and glucose
options.why: Protein and glucose in urine signal disease.

options.t: About 99% water, usually containing electrolytes only
options.why: That overstates the water fraction.

questions.stem: What moves urine out of the kidney and along the ureters?
questions.why: Urine is moved by peristaltic contractions beginning inside the kidney and the minor and major calyces. Those contractions continue in the renal pelvis and move urine along the ureters toward the bladder.

options.why: Filtration pressure is spent by the time urine reaches the ureter.

options.t: Gravity acting on the fluid column
options.why: Urine moves against gravity when lying down.
Ureteral movement is involuntary.

questions.stem: Approximately how long are the ureters?
questions.why: The ureters are thin-walled muscular tubes about 12 inches (30 cm) in length.

options.why: That overstates their length.
That is far shorter than the actual length.
That understates their length.

questions.stem: What is the path urine takes from the collecting ducts to the ureter?
questions.why: Urine enters the collecting ducts in the renal pyramids of the medulla, then passes through the minor calyx, into the major calyx, and then into the renal pelvis.

options.t: Collecting ducts, loop of Henle, renal pelvis, ureter
options.why: The loop of Henle comes before the collecting duct.

options.t: Collecting ducts, renal pelvis, major calyx, minor calyx, ureter
options.why: The calyces come before the renal pelvis.

options.t: Collecting ducts, minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter
Collecting ducts, renal cortex, renal medulla, ureter
options.why: Cortex and medulla are regions, not the drainage path.

questions.stem: What triggers the micturition reflex, and what does it cause?
questions.why: Stretching of the bladder walls stimulates nerve impulses producing the micturition reflex. This spinal reflex causes contraction of the bladder's smooth muscle.

options.t: Rising ureteral pressure; the bladder relaxes
options.why: Bladder stretch, not ureteral pressure, is the trigger.

options.t: Rising urine acidity; the bladder contracts
options.why: Acidity does not trigger the reflex.

options.t: Bladder wall stretch; smooth muscle contracts
Signals from the brain; the sphincter relaxes
options.why: The reflex is spinal; the brain only overrides it.

questions.stem: How does the urge to void arise, and what keeps urination from occurring immediately?
questions.why: The urge is produced by pressure exerted on the internal urinary sphincter. Normally the brain controls that urge, keeping the external urinary sphincter contracted until conditions are favorable.

options.t: Bladder stretch alone; gravity delays voiding
options.why: Stretch triggers the reflex but pressure creates the urge.

options.t: Internal sphincter pressure; brain holds external
External sphincter pressure; internal is held
options.why: The internal sphincter generates the urge.

options.t: Ureteral peristalsis; the pelvis delays voiding
options.why: The bladder, not the pelvis, generates the signal.

questions.stem: How does the bladder change shape as urine accumulates?
questions.why: When empty the bladder collapses and its muscular walls fold over onto themselves. As urine accumulates it expands and becomes pear-shaped.

options.t: Flattens progressively as it continues filling
options.why: It expands outward rather than flattening.

options.t: Collapses when empty, pear-shaped when full
Stays a fixed sphere and raises its pressure
options.why: It changes shape rather than holding one form.
It becomes pear-shaped, not conical.

questions.stem: Where does the dome of the bladder sit, and why does that matter anatomically?
questions.why: Most of the bladder rests in the anterior abdominal cavity, but its dome sits in the posterior abdominal cavity — the retroperitoneum — where the ureters and kidneys also reside.

options.t: Thoracic cavity, just above the diaphragm
options.why: The bladder sits well below the diaphragm.

options.t: Pelvic cavity, outside the peritoneum entirely
options.why: The dome specifically lies retroperitoneally.

options.t: Anterior abdomen, among the intestinal loops
options.why: Most of the bladder is anterior, but the dome is not.

questions.stem: What makes up the lower urinary tract?
questions.why: The urinary bladder and the urethra make up the lower urinary tract.

options.why: Both belong to the upper urinary tract.
The ureters belong to the upper tract.
The renal pelvis is part of the kidney.

questions.stem: What are the three regions of the male urethra, in order from the bladder?
questions.why: The prostatic urethra begins at the bladder and extends through the prostate gland; the membranous urethra runs from the prostate through the abdominal wall into the penis; the spongy (penile) urethra passes through the penis to the external opening.

options.why: This reverses the sequence entirely.
The spongy region is last, not second.
The prostatic region comes first, at the bladder.

questions.stem: How does the urethra differ anatomically between males and females?
questions.why: In males the urethra passes from the anterior base of the bladder through the penis. In females it opens in front of the vagina.

options.t: Males through the penis; females before the vagina
Males shorter than females by several inches
options.why: The female urethra is the shorter of the two.

options.t: Males before the scrotum; females via the uterus
options.why: The male urethra runs through the penis.

options.t: Females pass through the bladder wall twice
options.why: The female urethra passes in front of the vagina.

questions.stem: Which mechanism stimulates a person to take in more fluids when body fluids have decreased?
questions.why: Thirst stimulates intake when body fluids decrease. ADH allows fluid volume to build up, the kidneys activate to excrete excess, and water shifts move fluid between compartments.

options.why: That retains fluid already present.
That redistributes fluid between compartments.
That eliminates fluid rather than taking it in.

questions.stem: What happens when too many fluids enter the body?
questions.why: With fluid excess, thirst decreases, the kidneys are activated, and more urine is excreted, eliminating the surplus. More blood flowing to the kidneys — a larger fluid volume — stimulates that excretion.

options.t: The ureters dilate to speed drainage
options.why: Ureter calibre does not change with fluid load.

options.t: ADH rises to hold onto the extra volume
options.why: ADH falls when fluid is plentiful.

options.t: Water shifts entirely into the cells
options.why: Water shifts redistribute but do not eliminate excess.

options.t: Thirst falls, kidneys excrete more urine

questions.stem: What are water shifts?
questions.why: Water shifts move water from one compartment to another — extracellular and intracellular — and move unequal amounts of electrolytes into and out of the cells, all in an attempt at homeostasis.

options.t: Exchanging water between plasma and lymph
options.why: Water shifts involve intracellular compartments too.

options.t: Losing water through skin and lungs
options.why: That is insensible loss, not a compartment shift.

options.t: Moving urine from kidney to bladder
options.why: That is ureteral transport.

questions.stem: Match each nephron structure to its role.
questions.why: Filter, screen, reabsorb, fine-tune. The glomerulus does bulk filtration and everything downstream is about deciding what to keep.
pairs: Glomerulus
Capillary bed whose pores allow blood to be filtered
Glomerular capsule
Double-layered cup whose membrane blocks large proteins
Loop of Henle
Additional reabsorption of water and electrolytes
Distal convoluted tubule
Final adjustments under ADH and aldosterone control

questions.stem: Match each kidney region to its description.
questions.why: Outside in: capsule, cortex, medulla, pelvis. Nephrons live in the cortex; the pelvis is the collection point.
pairs: Renal cortex
Lighter-colored outer layer, closest to the fibrous capsule
Renal medulla
Middle layer forming cone-shaped renal pyramids
Renal pelvis
Collects urine and forms the upper portion of the ureter
Fibrous capsule
Envelops the kidney and protects it against infection

questions.stem: Match each fluid balance mechanism to its effect.
questions.why: Two mechanisms add volume (ADH retains, thirst adds), one removes it (kidneys), and one redistributes what is already there.
pairs: ADH
Allows fluid volume in the body to build up
Thirst
Stimulates intake of fluids when body fluids decrease
Kidneys
Stimulate excretion of fluids when volume is too large
Water shifts
Move water between extracellular and intracellular compartments
